# Copy from facts and the reader's next question

Use when creating interface text or when copy changes are authorized. A visual-only request preserves wording; report material copy issues separately. Read the whole sequence, not isolated sentences. A heading can be clear on its own and redundant after the heading above it.

## Assemble the factual material

Recover what the product provides, who it serves, the action available, its terms, the evidence supplied and its limits. Separate confirmed facts from assumptions and illustrative data. A familiar category does not license inventing customer counts, response times, integrations, reviews or pricing. If a fact is missing, omit the unsupported claim, design around the information available or ask when the outcome depends on it.

Keep a short fact sheet in working notes when writing a whole page. It should answer: what is offered, what the reader needs to decide, which details distinguish it, what would cause hesitation, what the next action actually does and what cannot be promised. This is source material, not a visitor-facing template to paste into every site.

The strongest detail is often ordinary and specific: collection is on Thursday, appointments take 40 minutes, exported data is CSV, the lift does not reach the top floor. Such details belong only when true. A fabricated inconvenience is as misleading as a fabricated benefit.

## Match the reader's stage

Someone unfamiliar with the category needs an understandable explanation. Someone comparing providers needs mechanism, terms and evidence. Someone already using the application needs a label and an action, not another introduction to the product. Do not make every operational screen read like a landing page.

Organize regions around distinct reader questions. An offer can explain what is provided, demonstrate it, resolve a relevant concern and give the next action. A record detail can identify the object, show its state, expose useful history and place actions near their consequences. The sequence follows content; there is no mandatory proof strip, feature grid or FAQ when no true material supports one.

## Set a usable voice

Use the client's own writing or confirmed brand direction when available. Otherwise choose a voice from audience, task and context. Technical language can be precise without being cold; a local service can be welcoming without a literary slogan; an error should be calm and actionable even if the marketing voice is playful.

Write a small voice note: preferred terms, point of view, sentence rhythm and places where personality belongs. Avoid cycling through synonyms for the same product object. If the application calls something an invoice, its filters, details and errors should not randomly call it a bill, receipt or payment.

Test whether a sentence would remain equally plausible after replacing the product name with an unrelated competitor. If so, identify what information is missing rather than merely swapping adjectives. “Tools that work as hard as you do” is not made specific by changing “tools” to “platform.”

## Work through examples

**Offer:** “A better way to work” leaves the category and action unresolved. With confirmed facts, a useful replacement could explain that the tool tracks unpaid invoices and upcoming expenses for independent consultants. This is longer but supplies information. Do not claim it predicts cash accurately unless the implementation and data support that promise.

**Section:** “Built for your everyday” above a record list adds little. A heading such as “Invoices awaiting payment” identifies the work. If the user protected the original wording, retain it and adjust presentation only; do not use the example as permission to rewrite.

**Action:** “Continue” can be correct when the next step is obvious and reversible. Where a consequence matters, name it: “Request a quote,” “Save draft” or “Delete invoice.” “Book now” is misleading if the form only sends an availability inquiry. A verb-and-object label is a useful default, not a rule to make already clear controls awkward.

**Error:** “Oops! Something went wrong” lacks a recovery. When the actual failure is an expired session, explain that the user must sign in again and whether the draft is retained. Do not promise retained data without checking. When the cause is unknown, be honest and provide the supported retry or help path.

**Empty result:** “Your journey starts here” is inappropriate after a search. “No invoices match these filters” and an available clear action answer the current problem. A genuinely new account may instead need first-use guidance.

**Confirmation:** “You're all set” can supplement a result but should not replace it. State what was saved or submitted and the next relevant step. A local demonstration says no message was sent rather than simulating a real booking receipt.

## Edit by contribution

Read heading, description, caption, note and footer together. Assign each a job. Remove or replace repeated reassurance only when copy is in scope. A sentence that restates the same promise in another metaphor is not new information. Preserve necessary legal language, safety instructions and deliberate campaign wording.

Keep labels short enough to scan but not so abbreviated that newcomers cannot understand them. Put supporting detail near the decision it changes. A tooltip or distant help page should not carry an essential price condition. Use full translatable messages rather than concatenating fragments whose grammar fails in another language.

Avoid turning anti-slop rules into a new uniform voice. Not every sentence must be short, every heading literal or every joke removed. Repetition, unsupported claims and generic promises are the issues; punctuation and individual words are weak evidence on their own. After editing, inspect whether the new wording became a sequence of monotonous fragments or sterile labels.

## Implementation and acceptance

Use the existing content system and keep user-controlled strings escaped or rendered safely by the framework. Check real wrapping in controls, narrow layouts and translated text. Confirm accessible names remain aligned with visible labels and that errors are associated with their fields. Do not replace a meaningful accessible name with a marketing slogan.

Verify the complete task using the text alone: what is this, what state am I in, what can I do, what will happen and how do I recover? Check every factual claim against its source and report unresolved material. Copy is successful when it helps the reader make the intended decision accurately, not when a lint or authorship detector says it sounds human.
